_comment: Edit this file to add or modify points of interest. Each POI needs: id (unique slug), name, name_ja (Japanese, optional), book (spring-snow | runaway-horses | temple-of-dawn | decay-of-the-angel), lat, lng, type, description. Types: residence, institution, shrine, district, natural, other.

pois.name: Matsugae Family Mansion
pois.description: The grand Meiji-era mansion of the Matsugae marquis family in Azabu, blending Western architecture with Japanese tradition. Kiyoaki grows up here surrounded by wealth and a sense of displacement from both worlds.

pois.name: Ayakura Family Residence
pois.description: Home of Count Ayakura and his daughter Satoko. A more traditional aristocratic household, steeped in Heian court culture and classical refinement, in contrast to the Matsugae's Westernized ostentation.

pois.name: Gakushūin (Peers' School)
pois.description: The school in Mejiro where Kiyoaki Matsugae and Shigekuni Honda study together. Reserved for sons of the aristocracy. Their friendship begins and deepens here.

pois.name: Kamakura
pois.description: Honda and Kiyoaki visit Kamakura together. Honda returns here at the novel's end, watching the sea and reflecting on loss and impermanence — the first intimation of the series' recurring themes of reincarnation.

pois.name: Gesshuji Convent
pois.description: A fictional Rinzai Buddhist convent set in the hills above Nara, where Satoko retreats and takes the tonsure. Honda's repeated attempts to see her here — always refused — form the novel's devastating final movement.

pois.name: Nara
pois.description: Ancient former capital, setting for Kiyoaki and Satoko's final meetings and Satoko's eventual withdrawal from the world. Honda visits repeatedly, unable to gain entry to the convent.

pois.name: Nanzenji Area, Kyoto
pois.description: The Higashiyama hills and the Nanzenji temple district provide the backdrop for Kiyoaki and Satoko's clandestine meetings, arranged through the Abbess's connections. The atmosphere is one of autumn beauty and forbidden longing.

pois.name: Hamarikyu / Shimbashi
pois.description: The fashionable Shimbashi district and the Hamarikyu gardens, part of the social and urban backdrop of Meiji-era Tokyo aristocratic life depicted in Spring Snow.

pois.name: Osaka District Court
pois.description: Honda, now a judge in his thirties, is posted at the Osaka District Court. It is here that he attends a kendo tournament and first encounters Isao Iinuma — a young man whose resemblance to Kiyoaki is uncanny.

pois.name: Iinuma Dojo
pois.description: The kendo dojo run by Iinuma, once the Matsugae family's stern retainer and Kiyoaki's tutor. Now a nationalist ideologue. His son Isao trains here, steeped in the purity doctrine of the Divine Wind league.

pois.name: Kenshindō Dojo
pois.description: The tournament venue where Honda first watches Isao compete. The moment of recognition — that Isao bears the same birthmarks as Kiyoaki — launches Honda's obsessive inquiry into reincarnation.

pois.name: Ise Grand Shrine
pois.description: The holiest site in Shinto, dedicated to Amaterasu. Isao's pilgrimage here is the spiritual climax of his ideological formation. The shrine's forest and river — absolute, eternal — intensify his conviction of divine mission.

pois.name: Mount Hiei
pois.description: Sacred mountain on the border of Kyoto and Shiga prefectures, seat of Enryakuji temple. Referenced in the nativist and Buddhist strands of Runaway Horses as a node of spiritual-national heritage.

pois.name: Imperial Palace Grounds, Tokyo
pois.description: The symbolic center of Isao's ideology. The Palace and its grounds represent the divine sovereignty the League of the Divine Wind seeks to restore. The assassination plot against financial oligarchs draws its justification from loyalty to the Emperor.

pois.name: Marunouchi District, Tokyo
pois.description: Tokyo's financial and commercial heart, including the Marunouchi Building (Marubiru, 1923). The industrial and banking interests based here are the targets of Isao's group — symbols of a Japan corrupted by capital and Western influence.

pois.name: Ginza
pois.description: Tokyo's most Westernized commercial district in the 1930s — department stores, cafés, Western fashions. For Isao's nationalist circle, Ginza represents the decadence they have sworn to purge.

pois.name: Miho no Matsubara / Suruga Bay Coast
pois.description: The pine-fringed coast on Suruga Bay near Shimizu, with views of Mount Fuji. Isao retreats here for the novel's final act. The sea and sky at dawn carry the novel's closing image of transcendence and self-destruction.

pois.name: Wat Arun (Temple of Dawn)
pois.name_ja: 暁の寺（ワット・アルン）
pois.description: The riverside Bangkok temple that gives the novel its title. Honda, now in his late forties and travelling in Thailand, visits the temple and encounters the young Princess Ying Chan, who claims — to the household's alarm — to remember a past life as a Japanese man.

pois.name: Thai Royal Palace, Bangkok
pois.description: Honda is received at the Thai court while on his diplomatic and legal travels. Princess Ying Chan, a young royal cousin, is the latest figure Honda suspects of carrying Kiyoaki and Isao's reincarnated soul, identifiable by the same three moles.

pois.name: Benares (Varanasi) and the Ganges
pois.description: On a side trip to India, Honda witnesses the burning ghats and bathers along the Ganges at dawn — a vision of cyclical death, decay, and rebirth that crystallizes the novel's meditation on the Buddhist doctrine of transmigration.

pois.name: Honda's Villa, Gotemba
pois.description: The country house Honda builds in the shadow of Mount Fuji. Years later, the now-grown Ying Chan visits during a stay in Japan; Honda's obsessive voyeurism here marks the novel's descent into moral corrosion. The villa recurs as the central setting of The Decay of the Angel.

pois.name: Karuizawa
pois.description: The fashionable mountain resort town where Honda's social circle summers. Ying Chan, studying in Japan, stays nearby — bringing Honda's reincarnation obsession back to Japanese soil after his travels in Thailand and India.

pois.name: Mio Signal Station, Shimizu
pois.description: The lonely lighthouse-keeper's signal station near Miho, overlooking the same Suruga Bay coastline where Isao died. Here the elderly Honda discovers Tōru Yasunaga, an orphaned sixteen-year-old he comes to believe is the next reincarnation.

pois.name: Honda's Villa, Gotemba (Tōru's Adoption)
pois.name_ja: 本多の御殿場別荘（透の養子縁組）
pois.description: Honda adopts Tōru and brings him to live at the Gotemba villa, grooming him as his heir and the latest vessel of the soul he has tracked across three lifetimes. The household's slow unraveling — Tōru's cruelty, Honda's decline — plays out here.

pois.name: Gesshūji Convent, Final Visit
pois.description: An aged Honda makes a final pilgrimage to the convent to see the now-elderly Abbess — once Satoko. Her quiet, devastating response to his life's obsession closes the tetralogy, casting the entire reincarnation narrative into doubt.

pois.name: Tōru's Tokyo Apartment
pois.description: After his falling-out with Honda, Tōru lives alone in Tokyo, increasingly isolated and embittered. His attempted suicide — drinking a chemical that blinds rather than kills him — marks the novel's cruelest turn.
